images.caption: Cover Illustration: Symmetry is visible in nature and expressed mathematically as invariance under transformation. Physical laws often possess important symmetries, while deeper symmetry-based explanations remain an area of research.
images.alt: Luminous sixfold crystal illustrates rotational symmetry, with natural forms and abstract physical patterns in a deep-blue cosmic scene.
images.description: An idealised six-armed ice-crystal motif is set within gold rotational geometry and a navy/cyan cosmic background. The image introduces symmetry in natural patterns and physical law; it does not establish that all phenomena arise from a single deeper physical mechanism.

images.caption: Figure 1.1: Symmetry appears in biological forms, crystals and idealised physical models. Living structures often display approximate balance, while mathematical symmetry concerns precise invariance under specified transformations.
images.alt: A butterfly, flower, leaf, snowflake, crystal lattice and magnetic-style field lines illustrate natural and physical symmetry.
images.description: The butterfly and leaf illustrate approximate bilateral patterning, alongside a flower and a stylised sixfold snowflake, a lattice model and idealised dipole-style field lines. These visual similarities arise from different mechanisms and do not themselves demonstrate a unified physical law.

images.caption: Figure 2.1: Sunflowers, shells, branching plants, crystals and water ripples display recurring forms created by distinct biological and physical processes. These are illustrative patterns, not measurements proving an exact golden-ratio relationship.
images.alt: Sunflower seed pattern, spiral shell, branching tree, sixfold snowflake and concentric water ripples illustrate different natural structures.
images.description: The image shows radial seed organisation in a sunflower, shell-like growth, a branched tree, an idealised sixfold ice crystal and spreading circular water waves. No golden rectangle or exact-fit spiral is asserted. Natural specimens are rarely perfectly symmetrical, and similarities of shape do not imply identical causes.

images.caption: Figure 3.1: An idealised sixfold form is unchanged by certain rotations and mirror reflections. Translating a finite form produces a congruent object in a new position; this is a transformation, not translational invariance of the original finite object.
images.alt: An idealised sixfold crystal retains its form after a sixty-degree rotation or mirror reflection, while translation moves it to a new position.
images.description: The central regular sixfold crystal demonstrates rotations of 60 degrees and mirror reflection as elements of its dihedral group D₆. In the separate translation example, x′ = x + a and y′ = y + b describe a new location; the moved finite shape has the same size and form but is not invariant at its original position. Extended periodic patterns can possess translation symmetry, but this isolated object does not.

images.caption: Figure 4.1: Noether's theorem connects continuous symmetries of a system's action with conserved quantities. The illustration focuses on rotational invariance and angular momentum; in the mechanical example, conservation requires no net external torque.
images.alt: A rotating celestial-style schematic and arrows link continuous rotational invariance through Noether's theorem to angular momentum conservation.
images.description: A luminous rotating object and schematic field curves appear beside a sequence reading continuous rotational symmetry, Noether's theorem and conserved angular momentum, represented as L = constant. Time translation and space translation relate to energy and linear momentum conservation, respectively, under the relevant assumptions; this artwork illustrates just the rotational case.

images.caption: Figure 5.1: Symmetric physical laws can admit lower-symmetry states during transitions. The lower V(φ) sketch is a one-dimensional schematic double-well, not a complete Mexican-hat field potential or a universal mass-generation model.
images.alt: A symmetric field pattern changes into differentiated domains during a phase transition, above a labelled double-well potential.
images.description: The visual transitions from a more uniform symmetric arrangement through a cooling/phase-change motif to an irregular pattern of distinct domains. Beneath it, a one-dimensional potential V(φ) shows a central high-energy point and two lower minima; this is an illustrative cross-section of state selection, not a complete model of the Higgs mechanism.

images.caption: Figure 6.1: SYMMETRIA asks whether deeper symmetry and constraints might help explain the emergence of physical structure. This proposed sequence is an exploratory, untested hypothesis—not established physics or experimental evidence of a unified theory.
images.alt: A luminous geometric core leads through hypothetical constraints and emergent structures toward observable patterns, labelled as an exploratory hypothesis.
images.description: A hypothetical progression is shown from hidden symmetry to constraints, emergent structure and observable patterns. Arrows suggest a proposed direction of explanation, not a demonstrated causal derivation. The artwork explicitly says 'Exploratory hypothesis — not established physics.' No distinctive SYMMETRIA prediction is claimed to have been confirmed.

figures.description: The visual transitions from a more uniform symmetric arrangement through a cooling/phase-change motif to an irregular pattern of distinct domains. Beneath it, a one-dimensional potential V(φ) shows a central high-energy point and two lower minima; this is an illustrative cross-section of state selection, not a complete model of the Higgs mechanism.
figures.caption: Figure 5.1: Symmetric physical laws can admit lower-symmetry states during transitions. The lower V(φ) sketch is a one-dimensional schematic double-well, not a complete Mexican-hat field potential or a universal mass-generation model.

figures.alt: A luminous geometric core leads through hypothetical constraints and emergent structures toward observable patterns, labelled as an exploratory hypothesis.
figures.description: A hypothetical progression is shown from hidden symmetry to constraints, emergent structure and observable patterns. Arrows suggest a proposed direction of explanation, not a demonstrated causal derivation. The artwork explicitly says 'Exploratory hypothesis — not established physics.' No distinctive SYMMETRIA prediction is claimed to have been confirmed.
figures.caption: Figure 6.1: SYMMETRIA asks whether deeper symmetry and constraints might help explain the emergence of physical structure. This proposed sequence is an exploratory, untested hypothesis—not established physics or experimental evidence of a unified theory.
